note: Read from tree-sitter-elixir's scanner.c, whose `serialize` is
`return 0`: elixir is the one grammar in the eight that carries no
state at all. Its twenty quoted bodies are a walk over one table of
against the bytes at the offset, and a table is what a book is. So
this book has no `kinds`, pushes nothing, and reads no organ - the
whole of it is twenty patterns and the order they are tried in.
That order is the C's, and it is load bearing twice: the first row
whose terminal the state admits wins, and a row that wins with an
empty body ends the ask rather than letting the next row try. Both
are stated below rather than assumed.
The remaining six externals - the three newline look-aheads, the two
unary-operator conditions and the quoted-atom start - are not here.
Every branch of each is a keyword read against `valid_symbols`, which
is a caller with a permission set rather than a scanner with memory,
and they sit behind their own hands for the same reason kotlin's four

rules.name: arbitrary_code_rather_than_a_quoted_body
rules.note: `find_quoted_token_info` opens by declining outright when the single- and double-quoted bodies are *both* admitted, because a state that would take either is not inside a string at all - it is reading code, and the twenty rows below would otherwise hand it the first row in the table. Guard rather than answer: it emits nothing and every row names it, which is the one thing a conjunction of tests cannot say about itself.

rules.name: i_single
rules.note: A single-quoted body without a heredoc's line rule: the run is every byte that is not the delimiter, `#{`, or any escape. A `#` not followed by `{` is content.

rules.name: i_single_holds_nothing
rules.note: The C returns `false` from `scan_quoted_content` when the body was empty, and a `false` there is not a fall-through: the row was chosen, so no other row is consulted. Without this the eleventh row could answer for the second at `''`.

rules.name: i_heredoc_single
rules.note: A single-quoted heredoc. The close is three 'single' bytes and *only* on a fresh line, so the run is tempered against `\n<blanks>'''` rather than against the byte - a lone or doubled "'" inside the body is content. The newline and the closing line's indent belong to the content, because the C marks the end after skipping them and before it looks at the delimiter. The other way out is `#{` or an escape that is not a line continuation.

rules.name: roll:quoted_atom_start
rules.note: scanner.c:608-616. The colon of `:"foo"`, and the whole branch: the C reaches it only under `valid_symbols[QUOTED_ATOM_START]`, advances one byte, marks the end there, and then *keeps the answer only if* a quote follows - so the token is the colon alone and the quote is the grammar's own. This lived in the Provision roll as a `:` with `after` of `"` and `'`, which is the same bytes and none of the permission.
